title: The man who sold the Eiffel Tower

hooks.text: This man sold the Eiffel Tower... for scrap metal.
In 1925, the Eiffel Tower had a buyer. It wasn't for sale.
How do you sell a landmark you don't own?
The easiest scam in history needed one newspaper.
This man sold the Eiffel Tower, and the buyer kept quiet.
Paris almost lost the Eiffel Tower to a con man.

hookVariants.visual: Tower close-up tilts up, the con man in front; SOLD stamp slams on 'scrap metal'.
Open on a FOR SALE sign hanging from the tower's leg, pull back to reveal the whole tower; con man tips his hat.
Open on a fat stack of cash in the con man's hands, rack focus to the tower behind him; SOLD stamp.

beats.text: This man sold the *Eiffel Tower*... for scrap metal.
beats.visual: Paris day. The tower towers over a smug con man (top hat, mustache). On 'Eiffel Tower' the camera tilts up the tower; on 'scrap' a giant SOLD stamp slams onto it.

beats.text: Paris, 1925. Victor Lustig is reading the paper when he spots a tiny story.
beats.visual: Cafe terrace. Lustig at a small table with a newspaper, coffee; camera glides in over his shoulder to the paper.

beats.text: The tower is rusting, and repainting it costs a *fortune.*
beats.visual: Newspaper close-up: headline TOWER NEEDS REPAIRS, a drawing of a rusty tower; on 'fortune' a price tag pops; Lustig's eyes narrow into a smug grin.

beats.text: So he forges *government* letterhead and becomes a deputy director at the Ministry of Posts.
beats.visual: Night, desk lamp. Lustig stamps official letterhead MINISTERE DES POSTES; a name badge DEPUTY DIRECTOR pops on his suit.

beats.text: He books a suite at the Hôtel de Crillon and invites *five* scrap dealers.
beats.visual: Grand hotel suite, red curtains, gold. Five dealers pop into chairs around a long table, one by one.

beats.text: His pitch: the city is secretly tearing the tower down. *Seven thousand tons* of iron.
beats.visual: Lustig at an easel with a tower drawing; a red X slashes it; counter 7,000 TONS slams in; dealers' faces go greedy.

beats.text: One dealer, André Poisson, wants it badly. But something feels off.
beats.visual: Close on Poisson (round glasses, mustache): greedy, then suspicious, eyes narrow; slow push.

beats.text: So Lustig makes a confession. He's a corrupt official, and he needs a *bribe.*
beats.visual: Lustig leans in and whispers behind his hand; on 'bribe' a BRIBE? speech card pops; Poisson's face relaxes into a grin.

beats.text: You see, to Poisson, the bribe was the proof. Only a real official would ask for one.
beats.visual: Poisson's thought bubble: a checkmark stamp REAL. Camera pushes.

beats.text: So Poisson pays $20,000, plus *$50,000* more to win.
beats.visual: A briefcase opens, bills burst out; counter $20,000 then $70,000 spins up.

beats.text: Within the hour, Lustig is on a train to *Vienna* with the cash.
beats.visual: Golden-hour station, a toy-like train pulls out; Lustig waves from the window with a bulging suitcase; sign VIENNA.

beats.text: He waits for the headlines. Nothing. Poisson is too *embarrassed* to report it.
beats.visual: Night hotel room in Vienna: Lustig flips newspapers, nothing; cut-in on Poisson facepalming, blushing.

beats.text: So Lustig comes back to Paris and tries to sell the tower *again.*
beats.visual: Back at the tower: Lustig with a new group of dealers, FOR SALE sign again.

beats.text: This time, the buyer calls the police, and Lustig escapes to *America.*
beats.visual: One dealer on a phone; police lights flash; Lustig sprints off toward a ship labelled TO AMERICA.

beats.text: But historians have never found a single police report. The only proof might be a con man's *word.*
beats.visual: Archive: a historian with a magnifier opens a drawer POLICE REPORTS 1925 - empty. Pull back to Lustig winking in front of the tower.
